Octahedral Coordination

02Why 6 or 8 nearest neighbors?

Same 1:1 stoichiometry, different packing: NaCl is 6:6 octahedral, CsCl is 8:8 cubic. One inverted polyhedron pair is highlighted in each structure.

SPECIMEN 03/03 · RADIUS-RATIO RULE

03Void geometry sets the coordination number

Treat ions as hard spheres: a stable packing needs cation–anion contact with no anion–anion contact. The ratio r₊/r₋ decides which void the cation can prop open — drag the slider and watch the coordination number switch.

OCTAHEDRAL LIMIT · √2 − 1 ≈ 0.414
r₊ + r₋ = √2 · r₋　⟹　r₊/r₋ = √2 − 1

Four anions touch in the equatorial plane; center-to-vertex is √2·r₋. Below this the cation rattles, the octahedron collapses, and CN drops to 4.

CUBIC LIMIT · √3 − 1 ≈ 0.732
r₊ + r₋ = √3 · r₋　⟹　r₊/r₋ = √3 − 1

Anions sit on the corners of a 2r₋ cube; body-center-to-vertex is √3·r₋. At r₊/r₋ ≥ 0.732 the cation touches all 8 corner anions at once.

The radius-ratio rule is an empirical hard-sphere model; covalency and polarization cause exceptions.
